deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the orbit-correction work for Pallas (symbol ⚴ on the previous page, 'Berechnung von den 5 Oppositionen'). The page continues that computation for the IInd (1803 Jul 1.93 Paris), IIIrd (1804 Sep 27.13) and IVth (1806 Jan 3.49) oppositions. It is the material Gauss later published in the Pallas memoir (Disquisitio de elementis ellipticis Palladis, 1810). For each opposition he computes the heliocentric longitude in the orbit from trial elements and compares it with the observed longitude reduced to the orbit. He also forms the linear 'equation of condition' in the corrections E (epoch of mean longitude), μ (mean daily motion), ω (longitude of perihelion) and φ (eccentricity angle, e = sin φ). The least-squares solution follows on the next page.

Trial elements (previous page): mean longitude 155°29'28.57'' at epoch 1802; n = 770.85842''/day (log 2.8869746); perihelion 146°29'53.76'' + 0.33216'' t (log 9.52135); φ = 4°29'41.95'' − 0.003285'' t (log 7.51655); node 80°53'17.29'' + 0.004052'' t (log 7.60763); inclination 10°37'35.45'' with a 0.001200''/day term (log 7.07941).

Scheme per opposition (t = days since epoch):
1. Mean motion and secular terms. log t + log n gives n t: II 422372.62'', III 771730.21'', IV 1128918.30''. The secular terms are 0.33216t, 0.003285t, 0.004052t, 0.0012t: II 182.00, 1.80, 2.22, 0.66; III 332.54, 3.29, 4.06, 1.20; IV 486.45, 4.81, 5.93, 1.76.
   - Hence φ_II = 4°29'40.15'', φ_III = 38.66'', φ_IV = 37.14''.
   - The numbers in parentheses (13375, 13373, 13370) are the complement of log cos φ, i.e. 0.0013375 etc.
   - Mean longitude L = 155°29'28.57'' + n t (mod 360°): II 272°49'1.19''; III 9°51'38.78''; IV 109°4'46.87''.
   - Perihelion π: II 146°32'55.76''; III 146°35'26.30''; IV 146°38'0.21''.
   - Mean anomaly M = L − π: II 126°16'5.43''; III 223°16'12.48''; IV 322°26'46.66''.
2. Kepler's equation, E_ecc − e'' sin E_ecc = M, with log e'' = log(206264.8 sin φ) = 4.20854 (log e = 8.89411).
   - II: E = 129°43'17.77'' (correction +3°27'12.34'').
   - III: E = 220°21'45.54'' (−2°54'26.94'').
   - IV: E = 319°31'58.26'' (−2°54'48.40'').
   - log e cos E and log(1 − e cos E) are formed: II 0.0212219, III 0.0251846, IV 0.0259(6)…
3. True anomaly from Gauss's formula sin ½(v − E) = sin ½φ · sin E · √(a/r), with √(a/r) = (1 − e cos E)^(−1/2). Here 8.5934160 = log sin ½φ and 0.0106109½ = ½ log(1 − e cos E).
   - II: v − E = +3°22'23.36'', v = 133°5'41.13''.
   - III: −2°49'36.67'', v = 217°32'8.87''.
   - IV: −3°0'25.25'', v = 316°31'33.01''.
   - Check: log sin v = log sin E − log(1 − e cos E) + log cos φ, and log cos v are also written (9.8634566, 9.8345523 for II).
4. Orbital longitude λ = v + π: II 279°38'36.89''; III 4°7'35.17''; IV 103°9'33.22''.
5. Jupiter perturbations.
   - Jupiter's mean longitude = tabular value at the start of the year + 299.2''/day (log 2.47605) × days elapsed. II: 173°11'5.9'' + 15°12'22.6'' (54742.6'' = 299.2 × 182.97 d) = 188°23'28.5''. III: 203°36'35.9'' + 22°27'20'' = 226°3'55.9''. IV: 264°17'38.4'' + 17'25.9'' = 264°35'4.3''.
   - Argument D = L_Pallas − L_Jup: II 84°25'32.7''; III 143°47'42.9''; IV 204°29'42.6''.
   - Further arguments and coefficient arithmetic follow. I cannot fully reconstruct the summation.
   - Results: perturbation in longitude II +9'4.25''; III −4'45.45''; IV +12'34.44''.
   - Computed longitudes: II 279°47'41.14''; III 4°2'49.72''; IV 103°22'7.66''.
6. Observed side. The observed opposition longitude λ_obs is reduced to the orbit by tan u = tan(λ_obs − Ω)/cos i (log cos i = 9.99249), then ℓ = u + Ω.
   - II: 279°29'35.70'' − 80°53'19.51'' = 198°36'16.19'' → u = 198°54'22.45'' → ℓ = 279°47'41.96''.
   - III: 283°22'44.45'' → 283°9'27.46'' → 4°2'48.81''.
   - IV: 22°7'46.18'' → 22°28'38.88'' → 103°22'2.10''.
   - Heliocentric latitude from tan β = sin(λ − Ω) tan i (log tan i ≈ 9.27328): II −3°25'31.74''; III −10°20'38.78''; IV +4°2'33.53''.
7. Differential coefficients, with λ = π + v(L − π).
   - ∂λ/∂E = dv/dM = cos φ/(1 − e cos E)²; ∂λ/∂ω = 1 − dv/dM; ∂λ/∂μ = t · dv/dM.
   - ∂λ/∂φ = sin E (2 − e² − e cos E)/(1 − e cos E)². The constant 1.993856 = 2 − e² is followed by addition of ∓e cos E (0.050079, 0.059704, 0.059606).
   - II: 0.90410, 0.09590, 495.38, +1.4258. III: 0.88774, 0.11226, 888.75, −1.1843. IV: 1.1273, −0.1273, 1651.(0), −1.4195.
   - Equations of condition, computed + corrections = observed:
     - 279°47'41.14'' + 495.38μ + 0.09590ω + 0.90410E + 1.4258φ = 279°47'41.96''
     - 4°2'49.72'' + 888.75μ + 0.11226ω + 0.88774E − 1.1843φ = 4°2'48.81''
     - 103°22'7.66'' + 1651.7μ − 0.1273ω + 1.1273E − 1.4195φ = 103°22'2.10''

I checked all the anomaly, motion, reduction and coefficient arithmetic I could recompute; it agrees to the last place within my precision.
errors: IV opposition: the μ-coefficient is written 1651.7. From the page's own logs, 0.05204 + 3.16569 = 3.21773, which gives 1651.0 (= 1464.495 × 1.1273). Either a small slip by Gauss or a misreading of '1651,0'. The effect is negligible: about 0.7 × μ ≈ 0.05''.

II opposition: the mean longitude appears as 272°49'1.19'' in the main column but 272°49'1.27'' in the Jupiter-argument column. This is a trivial inconsistency with no effect on the perturbation argument.

Jupiter perturbation summations (left columns, e.g. −171.65, +721.90, +3719, +1023, +4742, 340.28 for II; −569.60, −2142, +1984, −158 for III; −3378, −2311.6, −5689.6 for IV) could not be fully reconstructed. I cannot verify the totals +544.25'', −285.45'', +754.44''.

results.what: Solution of Kepler's equation and conversion to true anomaly via sin½(v−E) = sin½φ sinE √(a/r)
results.usually_credited_to: Kepler; the half-angle formula is in Gauss, Theoria Motus (1809)

results.what: Partial derivatives of orbital longitude w.r.t. epoch, mean motion, perihelion and eccentricity angle (dv/dM = cosφ/(1−e cosE)², dv/dφ = sinE(2−e²−e cosE)/(1−e cosE)²)
results.modern_name: Differential correction of orbital elements (equations of condition)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th–19th c. astronomy; Gauss's form in Theoria Motus and the 1810 Pallas memoir

results.what: Reduction of opposition longitude to the orbit plane (tan u = tan(λ−Ω)/cos i) and heliocentric latitude (tan β = sin(λ−Ω) tan i)
Equations of condition for Pallas oppositions, later solved by least squares (next page)
results.modern_name: Least-squares orbit determination (Gaussian elimination appears in the 1810 Pallas paper)

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine working computations for the Pallas orbit correction that Gauss published in 1810. Nothing here goes beyond known methods of his.
